blocks.c: Chapter Fourteen: Lowspire
They came out of the cloud at four hundred feet and there it was.
Sol's first thought, which she was ashamed of for years afterwards, was that it was smaller than it should have been.

Lowspire hung in the clear air under the cloudline: a platform of black iron and grey timber, eleven-sided, perhaps four hundred feet across, with a shanty town grown over it like moss on a stone. Chimneys. Washing lines strung between chimneys, in the still air, holding actual washing. A dozen roofs of tarred canvas and a dozen more of slate that had plainly been carried down one sheet at a time. The old winding gear of the mine stood at one end, stripped to its ribs.
And in the middle, on a stone plinth that was the only stone in the whole structure, under a shingle roof on four posts: a bell.
It was the size of a kneeling person. Even from a quarter-mile Sol knew the shape of it, the way you know a relative's walk at a distance. She had rung its twin four times a day for three years.
Below the platform, in the dark, the iron went down and down in a lattice into the cinder-cliff, and the whole thing was very obviously not sitting on anything.
"It's hanging," said Dov, in the voice of a man watching his own arithmetic breathe. "Look at the frame. Look at the sag on the north side. That is a structure being held up, right now, by a note."
"By our note," said Sallow.
"By a note," said Roake.

The Sprat put down on a landing stage that had been built for boats twice her size and maintained by people with more will than materials. Sol saw the repairs first: a stringer spliced with a mine rail. A stanchion made from a chapel gate. A whole section of decking laid in mismatched planks, sanded, oiled, and kept better than the Gull's own.
Then she saw the people.

There were perhaps sixty of them on the stage and coming down the ways towards it, and they were not what she had braced for. She had braced for something out of a broadsheet: hollow faces, rags, the picturesque misery that towns tell each other about. What she got was sixty people in patched but mended clothes, most of them staring at the Sprat with the exact expression of a household hearing an unexpected knock at eleven at night.
A man at the front had a lamp and no weapon and was so frightened that his hand shook the light.
"You're not the mail," he said.
"No," said Sallow, stepping onto the stage as though he did this every day. "Though I notice that you expect mail, which is interesting, and which I shall be putting in my report."
"Sallow," said Roake.
"Bosun."

"Shut up." Roake stepped past him, took her hat off, and said, to the man with the lamp, in a voice Sol had never heard her use: "My name is Tamsin Roake. I'm bell-master of the Meridian Gull. I'd like to speak to Ysolde Kerrin, if she's here, and if she isn't I'll wait, and if you'd rather we went back up we'll go back up. We're not the Company. There's no Company on this boat."
The man's lamp steadied a little.
"You're Tamsin," he said.
"I am."

"She said you'd come." He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "She's said it every year since I was a boy. Every midsummer, when we ring the long one, she says: one of these years Tamsin Roake is going to work it out and come down that ladder, and when she does, mind your manners, because she'll have earned it."
They walked up through the town, and Sol looked at everything, and everything she looked at rearranged something in her head.

A school. Eleven children in it, at that hour, because school on Lowspire ran at night when the air was still. A chandler's shop with four items in the window and all four of them clean. A chapel that had plainly been two chapels once and had been made into one by the simple expedient of knocking a wall down, which suggested a story Sol wanted very badly to hear.
A washing line with a child's shirt on it, and a woman taking it in, and the woman stopped with the shirt in her hands and stared at Sol's uniform with her mouth open.

And under everything, felt in the soles of the feet rather than heard, the long steady hum of a bell that had been rung true a quarter of an hour ago and would be rung true again in eight hours, holding four hundred feet of iron and two hundred and eleven people in the air over a cinder-cliff.
Sol stopped in the middle of the street.
"Bosun," she said.
"I know."
"They're standing on our carry."
"I know," said Roake. "Keep walking. And Ferrant — get your face in order. Whatever we do about this, we do not do it while looking at these people as if they were a sum."
The thing Sol could not get past was the quiet.

Not silence — Lowspire was not silent; there were voices, and a hand-loom going somewhere, and the small constant noise of two hundred people living on four hundred feet of platform. It was that every noise on that platform had been made small on purpose. Doors were eased shut. Buckets were set down rather than dropped. A man came past with a barrow and Sol realised, after he had gone, that the barrow had rags bound round the rim of its wheel.
She said so to the man with the lamp, whose name turned out to be Wren Beck — the engineer's son, born on the platform, forty years old and the nearest thing Lowspire had to a mayor.

"Vibration bleeds carry," he said, as if reciting a table. "Bleeds it faster than you would think. My father worked it out in the first year, when we were dropping a foot a week. Everything that shakes costs us height."
"So you stopped everything that shakes."
"We stopped everything we could and we slowed everything we couldn't." He shrugged. "Children learn it at four. There's a rhyme for it."
"Say it."
He looked embarrassed, and then he said it, in the flat sing-song of a thing learned before memory:

Soft on the boards and soft on the stair,
soft with the door and the pail and the chair.
Loud is a shilling and shillings are dear,
and the ones who were loud are no longer here.
Sol stood in the middle of a street in a town in the sky and did not trust herself to speak for some time.
"That last line," she managed.
"Aye," said Wren Beck. "That one's not about vibration."
